body.heading: Fingers with place value
paragraphs: Ordinary finger counting wastes your hands: ten fingers, ten numbers. Give each finger a value instead - thumb 1, index 2, middle 4, ring 8, little finger 16 - and raise fingers so their values sum to the number you want. Thirteen, for example, is 8 + 4 + 1: ring finger, middle finger and thumb up, the rest down. Every number from 0 to 31 has exactly one pattern of raised fingers.

This is binary, the counting system computers use, where each digit is just 'on' or 'off'. Your five fingers are five binary digits - five bits - and 2 to the power 5 gives the 32 combinations, 0 through 31. Nothing about it is approximate: it is ordinary counting with a stricter, cleverer code.

body.heading: Both hands: a thousand numbers
paragraphs: Add your other hand and keep doubling: the second hand's fingers stand for 32, 64, 128, 256 and 512. With ten fingers you can show any number from 0 to 1,023 - that is 2 to the power 10, or 1,024 combinations. A thousand numbers, silently, on two hands.

Why do computers bother with binary at all? Because two states - on or off, high voltage or low - are far easier to build reliably than ten. Your fingers make the same trade: a finger is unambiguously up or down, so the code never smudges. Reliability, not elegance, is why the digital world counts in twos.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Practise counting from 0 to 31 on one hand, in order, without looking. The tricky moments are the carries - going from 7 (1+2+4) to 8 means three fingers drop and one rises, exactly like the 9-to-10 flip in ordinary counting. Smooth carries mean you have understood binary, not memorised it.

Then play the signalling game: stand across a room and send a friend numbers up to 31 on one hand, while they decode by adding finger values. Graduate to two hands and send your age, your house number, or a secret code below 1,024.

takeaway: Each finger doubles the count: five fingers reach 31, ten reach 1,023 - binary is just counting with two choices per finger.
